input.instructions: Create a compact, accurate blueprint for an 8-to-12-minute educational lesson with exactly ten sequential teaching beats. Do not write full narration. Create exactly three measurable learning objectives. For every beat, provide one distinct complete factual claim, a concrete example, a concise editable visual direction, and one or two exact supplied source IDs. End the claim, example, and visual direction with complete punctuation. Every cited source excerpt must directly support the claim; reuse at least two important technical terms from each cited excerpt so support can be checked locally. Do not invent course assignments, policies, measurements, datasets, instruction encodings, or product behavior that is absent from the supplied excerpts. Keep the claim, example, and visual direction compact; a deterministic local expander will produce the full narration. Sequence the beats from foundations through application and end with a practical analysis checklist. Use only the supplied source excerpts for factual claims. Every factual claim must cite one or more supplied source IDs. Narration must describe information that is essential to understand visuals. Do not imitate a named creator or invent sources.
input.prompt:
Topic: CSCI-243: The Mechanics of Programming. Create a representative course-foundations companion aligned to the official catalog description. It must teach durable concepts and problem-solving methods without claiming to replace the instructor's syllabus. Official catalog description: Students will be introduced to the details of program structure and the mechanics of execution as well as supportive operating system features. Security and performance issues in program design will be discussed. The program translation process will be examined. Programming assignments will be required. Prerequisite: C- or better in CSCI-140 or CSCI-142 or CSCI-242 or SWEN-124 or CSEC-124 or GCIS-124 or GCIS-127 or equivalent course. Contact Hours: Lecture 3 Typically Offered: Fall, Spring, Summer Every beat must be directly relevant to that catalog description. Prefer the RIT catalog source for scope claims. Use a supplemental source only when its cited claim teaches a named course topic; never use an unrelated source merely to fill a claim slot. Keep production directions exclusively in visualDirection and never say phrases such as 'on screen', 'show on screen', 'cut to', or 'camera' in narration. Regeneration revision 4: use ten distinct, specific beat titles and avoid repeating any title or section label.

Source excerpts:

[opendsa-programming-foundations]
Programming begins with precise problem statements, input and output examples, and algorithms written independently of syntax. Variables represent values and state, expressions compute values, and control structures select or repeat operations. Functions decompose a solution into named operations with parameters and results. Recursion solves a problem through smaller instances and requires a base case. Lists represent ordered sequences, stacks use last-in first-out access, queues use first-in first-out access, trees represent hierarchy, and graphs represent connected entities. Searching and sorting algorithms depend on representation and invariants. Correctness arguments, tests, tracing, and debugging compare intended behavior with observable results, including boundary and error cases.

[python-language-reference]
The Python language reference specifies lexical analysis, data model behavior, execution, expressions, statements, functions, classes, exceptions, and module import semantics. Python objects have identity, a type, and a value. Names are bound to objects within namespaces and scopes. Expressions produce values, while statements control execution and bindings. Exceptions interrupt normal control flow until a matching handler processes them or they propagate. The import system searches for modules and binds loaded modules into a namespace. Programs should be reasoned about through explicit state, control flow, data representation, contracts, tests, and observable behavior. Debugging separates syntax, runtime, and logical failures, while decomposition and abstraction reduce the number of interacting concerns.

[rit-csci-243]
Students will be introduced to the details of program structure and the mechanics of execution as well as supportive operating system features. Security and performance issues in program design will be discussed. The program translation process will be examined. Programming assignments will be required. Prerequisite: C- or better in CSCI-140 or CSCI-142 or CSCI-242 or SWEN-124 or CSEC-124 or GCIS-124 or GCIS-127 or equivalent course. Contact Hours: Lecture 3 Typically Offered: Fall, Spring, Summer

beats.claim: CSCI-243 introduces students to program structure, execution mechanics, OS features, security, performance, and the translation process, with prerequisites including CSCI-140 or C-
beats.example: A student enrolling in CSCI-243 must have earned a C- or better in CSCI-140, CSCI-142, CSCI-242, or an equivalent course such as SWEN-124.
beats.title: Defining the Scope of CSCI-243
beats.visualDirection: Display the official catalog description text in a centered box with a subtle border; highlight the prerequisite list in a contrasting color.

beats.claim: Programming begins with precise problem statements, input/output examples, and algorithms written independently of syntax.
beats.example: Before coding, a student writes a problem statement: 'Given a list of integers, return the sum of all positive values,' and provides sample inputs/outputs.
beats.title: The Foundation of Precise Problem Statements
beats.visualDirection: Show a split-screen: left side contains the written problem statement and examples; right side shows a blank editor window ready for algorithm pseudocode.

beats.claim: Variables represent values and state; expressions compute values; control structures select or repeat operations.
beats.example: In Python, `x = 5` binds a variable, `x + 3` is an expression evaluating to 8, and `if x > 0:` is a control structure that repeats or branches based on the condition.
beats.title: Core Building Blocks: Variables, Expressions, and Control
beats.visualDirection: Render three distinct code snippets side-by-side, each labeled 'Variable', 'Expression', and 'Control Structure', with syntax highlighting.

beats.claim: Functions decompose a solution into named operations with parameters and results, enabling modular design.
beats.example: A function `def sum_positive(nums):` takes a list parameter and returns a single integer result, isolating the summation logic.
beats.title: Functions as Decomposed Operations
beats.visualDirection: Illustrate a flowchart where a large problem box splits into smaller boxes, each labeled with a function name and its parameters.

beats.claim: Recursion solves a problem through smaller instances and requires a base case to terminate.
beats.example: The factorial function `def fact(n): if n == 0: return 1; return n * fact(n-1)` uses the base case `n == 0` to stop infinite recursion.
beats.title: Recursion and Base Cases
beats.visualDirection: Show a tree diagram where each node represents a recursive call, with the root labeled `fact(5)` and leaves labeled `1` (the base case).

beats.claim: Lists represent ordered sequences; stacks use last-in first-out access; queues use first-in first-out access; trees represent hierarchy; graphs represent connected entities.
beats.example: A stack of plates is popped from the top (LIFO), while a line of customers at a ticket booth is served from the front (FIFO).
beats.title: Data Structures: Lists, Stacks, Queues, Trees, Graphs
beats.visualDirection: Present five small diagrams: a horizontal list, a vertical stack with arrows pointing down, a queue with arrows pointing right, a binary tree, and a simple graph with nodes and edges.

beats.claim: Searching and sorting algorithms depend on representation and invariants that must hold throughout execution.
beats.example: Binary search maintains the invariant that the target, if present, lies within the current search interval; quicksort maintains partition invariants to guarantee sorted output.
beats.title: Searching, Sorting, and Invariants
beats.visualDirection: Animate a step-by-step binary search on a sorted array, highlighting the shrinking interval and the invariant condition at each step.

beats.claim: Python undergoes lexical analysis, parsing, and execution; the language reference specifies these stages and the data model behavior.
beats.example: The string `'def hello(): pass'` is tokenized into identifiers, keywords, and delimiters during lexical analysis, then parsed into an abstract syntax tree before the interpreter executes it.
beats.title: The Python Translation Pipeline
beats.visualDirection: Show a linear pipeline graphic: Source Code → Lexical Analyzer → Parser → AST → Bytecode → Interpreter → Output, with brief labels under each stage.

beats.claim: Python objects have identity, type, and value; names are bound to objects within namespaces and scopes, and the import system binds modules accordingly.
beats.example: When `import math` runs, the module object is created, and the name `math` is bound in the current namespace, allowing access to `math.sqrt(4)`.
beats.title: Namespaces, Scopes, and Object Identity
beats.visualDirection: Display a Venn diagram with overlapping circles labeled 'Global Scope', 'Local Scope', and 'Module Namespace', with a small icon representing an imported module inside the module circle.

beats.claim: Correctness arguments, tests, tracing, and debugging compare intended behavior with observable results, including boundary and error cases.
beats.example: A test suite includes a case where the input list is empty (boundary) and another where the list contains negative numbers (error handling), and tracing reveals the function returns 0 for the empty case.
beats.title: Debugging and Correctness: Tests, Tracing, and Boundaries
beats.visualDirection: Show a split view: left side lists test cases (including boundary and error inputs), right side displays a trace log with line numbers and variable states for each case.

learningObjectives: Identify the core components of program structure (variables, expressions, control structures, functions) and explain their roles in algorithm design.
Trace the program translation process from source code through lexical analysis, parsing, and execution, citing Python-specific mechanisms.
Apply debugging and correctness techniques (tests, tracing, boundary analysis) to evaluate program behavior against intended specifications.
